h.en: Stateless HTTP and the Cookie Round Trip

body.en:
HTTP is stateless: one request does not automatically remember what happened on the previous page. Cookies and sessions add continuity for preferences, shopping carts and login.

  • A cookie is a small name/value record stored by the browser for a site. PHP sends a Set-Cookie response header; the browser later sends the applicable value in a Cookie request header.
  • setcookie() queues that response header. $_COOKIE describes the incoming request, so it is not automatically updated by the call. Read the new value after a reload or redirect.
  • Cookie values are strings; PHP can encode/decode them for HTTP transport. They are not encrypted by setcookie, and the user can inspect, edit, block or delete them.
  • Run cookie programs through http://localhost/... under XAMPP or php -S localhost:8000, not by opening the PHP file directly. The CLI alone has no browser to store and return a cookie.
  • Our verified transcripts use curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt: read incoming cookies from a jar and save response cookies back to that same jar.

h.en: Creating, Reading, Updating and Destroying Cookies

body.en:
The options-array form is setcookie($name, $value, $options). The older positional form supplies expiry, path, domain, secure and httponly separately; the options array is clearer and also supports SameSite.

<?php
// Before HTML, echo or other output:
setcookie("city", "Surat", [
    "expires" => time() + 3600,
    "path" => "/",
    "httponly" => true,
    "samesite" => "Lax"
]);
// New value arrives on the NEXT request:
$city = $_COOKIE["city"] ?? "not selected";
echo htmlspecialchars($city);
  • Create: give the cookie a name, string value, expiry and scope. time() + 3600 is an absolute timestamp one hour from now, not a duration by itself.
  • Read: use $_COOKIE['city'] ?? 'default' or an isset check. Missing cookies are normal, not a reason for an undefined-key warning.
  • Update: set the same name/domain/path again with a new value and expiry. A different path may create a second cookie rather than replace the first.
  • Delete: set that same cookie with an expiry in the past. unset($_COOKIE['city']) only removes an entry from this script's array; it sends no deletion instruction to the browser.
  • Before output: setcookie, header and session-start operations must precede HTML, echo and accidental whitespace/BOM output. A true return from setcookie means the header was queued, not that the browser accepted it.
<?php
// Use the SAME name, path and domain as creation.
setcookie("city", "", [
    "expires" => time() - 3600,
    "path" => "/",
    "httponly" => true,
    "samesite" => "Lax"
]);
// Browser stops sending it on the next request.

h.en: Cookie Lifetime, Scope and Safe Preferences

body.en:
OptionPurpose and practical rule
expiresFuture timestamp = persistent cookie, subject to browser policy; 0/omitted = browser-session cookie. Browser session restore may preserve session cookies.
pathURL paths that receive the cookie. Use / for a whole-site preference. A path is routing scope, not a security boundary.
domainOmit for host-only scope. Set a wider domain only if subdomain sharing is actually needed.
secureSend over HTTPS only. Enable for production HTTPS; these local plain-HTTP examples do not require Secure.
httponlyStops JavaScript from reading the cookie through document.cookie; it does not eliminate every XSS attack.
samesiteLax/Strict/None controls cross-site sending. None requires Secure. SameSite is useful defence-in-depth, not a replacement for CSRF tokens.
  • Good cookie data: language, theme, last selected city. Bad data: passwords, trusted roles, bank balances or an unprotected login flag.
  • Browsers impose small per-cookie limits (roughly 4 KB, including overhead) and other count/size policies. Do not use cookies as a large database.
  • Validate every received value against an allowlist. A theme form should accept only light/dark, even if the normal HTML dropdown offers only those choices.
  • Post/Redirect/Get: process POST, set the cookie, send a 303 Location header, exit; the redirected GET can read the newly returned cookie.

h.en: Creating a Session and Sharing Data Between Pages

body.en:
A PHP session stores per-visitor data on the server and normally uses a browser cookie, typically PHPSESSID, to carry an opaque session ID. The ID is a lookup key, not the session's user/cart data.

<?php
session_start();  // before output, on EACH page
$_SESSION["user"] = "Ravi";
$_SESSION["seats"] = 2;
// On another page, after session_start():
echo htmlspecialchars($_SESSION["user"] ?? "Guest");
  • session_start() creates a session or resumes an existing one using the incoming ID; call it before output on every participating page. Calling it on a second page does not necessarily start a new visitor.
  • Set variables with $_SESSION['key'] = $value. Unlike cookie values, session data can contain arrays, numbers and other serialisable application values.
  • After starting the session, another page reads the same keys. Use ?? defaults or isset for first visits and logged-out users.
  • PHP's default handler stores data in server-side files; deployments may use a database or another session store. The browser receives only the identifier unless your application explicitly sends more.
  • Two browsers with different IDs normally have different sessions. A new incognito window is useful for testing isolation.
  • With a cookie-only configuration, a client that refuses the session cookie cannot retain the same session across separate requests. Do not put session IDs into URLs as a workaround.

h.en: Removing Session Variables and Destroying a Session

body.en:
OperationWhat it actually does
unset($_SESSION['theme'])Removes only that key; user/cart and the session remain.
session_unset() or $_SESSION = []Clears all variables in the active session, not the browser cookie or the session identity.
session_destroy()Destroys the server-side session data. It does not itself clear the current $_SESSION array or remove the browser's session cookie.

Complete logout: start/resume the session, clear the in-memory data, expire its cookie with matching scope, destroy the server-side record, then redirect and exit.

<?php
session_start();
unset($_SESSION["theme"]); // one key only
// Full logout is a DIFFERENT operation:
$_SESSION = [];
$p = session_get_cookie_params();
setcookie(session_name(), "", [
    "expires" => time() - 3600,
    "path" => $p["path"], "domain" => $p["domain"],
    "secure" => $p["secure"],
    "httponly" => $p["httponly"],
    "samesite" => $p["samesite"] ?? "Lax"
]);
session_destroy();
  • Do not confuse session_regenerate_id(true) with logout: it rotates the identifier while preserving current session values and invalidates the old session record.
  • Do not rely on closing the browser for authentication expiry. Cookies can be restored, and old server-side data may survive until garbage collection.
  • Real applications enforce idle/absolute expiry explicitly using timestamps stored in the session. If expired, perform the same full logout and require authentication again.
  • The verified program separately demonstrates one-key removal, clearing all values while the session stays active, and complete destruction followed by a new empty visit.

h.en: Protected Login, Session Fixation Defence and Logout

body.en:
Practical 16 requires more than storing a name: an unauthenticated visitor must not be able to open a protected page, even by typing its URL directly.

  1. Common config: enable strict mode and cookie-only IDs, set cookie parameters, then call session_start before any output.
  2. Login: accept a POST, verify its CSRF token, validate credentials using a password hash and password_verify. Never trust a hidden field or a cookie saying logged_in=1.
  3. Success: call session_regenerate_id(true) to reduce session-fixation risk, store a user ID/name in $_SESSION, then redirect to the dashboard.
  4. Guard: check the server-side authentication key on every protected request, before producing any private content. Redirect and exit if it is missing.
  5. Logout: use a POST with a valid CSRF token; clear variables, expire the session cookie, destroy the session, redirect to login and exit.
<?php
session_start();
if (!isset($_SESSION["user"])) {
    header("Location: login.php", true, 303);
    exit; // never render the protected body
}
// Only authenticated requests reach this line.
  • CSRF token: a random server-generated value stored in the session and echoed into the form. Compare it with hash_equals on submission. It helps reject a forged request from another site.
  • Session fixation means making a victim authenticate under an attacker-known ID. Strict mode rejects uninitialised IDs, and regeneration changes the ID after login.
  • Session hijacking means stealing a valid ID. HTTPS, Secure/HttpOnly cookies, suitable SameSite policy and prompt logout help; sessions are not automatically secure just because data lives on the server.
  • Run the program: save its four labelled sections as login.php, config.php, dashboard.php and logout.php. Open login.php through the server; lab credentials are ravi / demo@123. Database-backed credentials arrive in Unit 5.

h.en: Cookies vs Sessions: Choosing the Right Storage

body.en:
AspectCookie valuePHP session data
Stored atBrowserServer-side session store
Sent with requestApplicable cookie's valueNormally an opaque ID in a cookie
Typical capacitySmall per-cookie browser limitGoverned by server storage/configuration
LifetimeExpiry and browser policyApplication expiry, storage lifetime and garbage collection
TrustClient may edit the valueServer controls stored values, but the ID can still be stolen
Best useTheme/language preferenceAuthenticated user, cart, temporary workflow data
  • They are related mechanisms, not mutually exclusive alternatives: PHP sessions usually use a cookie for the session identifier.
  • A persistent preference cookie can survive longer than an authenticated session without keeping the visitor logged in.
  • A secure persistent remember-me login needs carefully designed expiring, revocable tokens; it is not a plaintext username/password cookie.
  • Both fail if the application exposes private data in HTML without checking access. Server-side storage is one part of security, not the whole design.

h.en: try, throw, catch and finally: The Control Flow

body.en:
An exception is an object reporting a failure that interrupts normal execution. Instead of checking a return code at every nested call, code can throw an exception and let a suitable caller handle it.

<?php
try {
    if ($count <= 0) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException(
            "Count must be positive."
        );
    }
    echo $total / $count;
} catch (InvalidArgumentException $e) {
    echo htmlspecialchars($e->getMessage());
} finally {
    // Close resources here; avoid return/exit.
}
  • try: surround operations that may throw. A try requires at least a catch or a finally.
  • throw: throw an exception object such as new InvalidArgumentException('bad count'). It immediately skips remaining statements in the try and searches outward for a matching catch.
  • catch: receives the exception in a variable, e.g. $e. $e->getMessage() gives its description; getCode(), getFile() and getLine() help diagnostics.
  • finally: runs cleanup after the normal try or the catch, including when a return or propagated exception leaves the block. Abrupt termination such as exit/die or killing the process can prevent it.
  • If handled without rethrow/return, execution continues after the structure. If there is no matching handler, the exception propagates to the caller; unhandled at the top level it terminates the request.
  • The fare program tests both a normal division and an invalid zero-passenger request, making the skipped line and the shared finally visible.

PHP provides Exception, InvalidArgumentException, RuntimeException and other standard classes. Extend a suitable class when callers need to recognise a particular domain failure.

<?php
class SeatsUnavailable extends RuntimeException {}
try {
    throw new SeatsUnavailable("Route is full.");
} catch (SeatsUnavailable $e) {
    echo "Choose another departure.";
} catch (Exception $e) {
    // Broad parent comes LAST, not first.
    error_log($e->getMessage());
    echo "Booking could not be completed.";
}
  • The booking program distinguishes invalid input (zero seats) from a legitimate request that cannot be fulfilled (too few seats available).
  • Only the first compatible catch runs. Put specific subclasses before broad parents such as Exception; otherwise the broad catch absorbs the specific case.
  • Different catches can take different actions: ask for corrected input, offer another departure, or log an unexpected failure.
  • throw $e; in a catch rethrows to an outer handler, useful when local code cannot recover.
  • Do not silently catch and ignore failures. Log diagnostic details securely and show a safe user-facing message; internal file paths and stack traces should not be exposed on a production site.

• Opening a file, acquiring a lock or beginning another resource-dependent operation creates a cleanup obligation. Putting cleanup only at the end of try misses the exception path.
  • Initialise the handle before try, open/work inside try, and in finally close it only if is_resource($h). This also handles failures before the open.
  • A successful return does not normally skip finally; a return inside finally can override the intended return or pending exception. Keep finally dedicated to cleanup.
  • Many PHP file functions produce a warning and return false, not an exception. Check the documented return value and explicitly throw if you want exception-based application flow.
  • The manifest program runs three cases against real files: success, failure after opening, and an unavailable file before opening. Its output confirms two closures and one no-handle cleanup.
  • A catch without finally is allowed, and try/finally without catch is also allowed when cleanup is needed but recovery belongs to the caller.

h.en: Exception, Error and Throwable in Modern PHP

body.en:
In PHP 7+, throwable failures have two major families, both implementing the Throwable interface:

FamilyExamplesCatching it
ExceptionRuntimeException, InvalidArgumentException and your subclassescatch (Exception $e), or a more specific exception type
ErrorTypeError, DivisionByZeroError and related engine errorscatch (Error $e), or a more specific error type
BothAny object implementing Throwablecatch (Throwable $t)
  • Exception does not include Error. A raw 10 / 0 raises DivisionByZeroError; the earlier fare validator instead deliberately throws an InvalidArgumentException before division.
  • Ordinary warnings/notices are not automatically throwable. A broad catch is not a universal replacement for checking function returns or validating input.
  • The strict-types program generates a real application exception, division error and type error, then proves the broad Throwable catch can also catch a TypeError.
  • Prefer specific, expected handlers close to the operation; use a broad boundary handler to log unexpected failures and return a safe error response, not to conceal programming bugs.

title.en: Create, read and update a cookie (Practical 17)

code.en:
<?php
$incoming = $_COOKIE["city"] ?? "(missing)";
$queued = null;
if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST") {
    $city = $_POST["city"] ?? "";
    if (!in_array($city, ["Surat", "Vadodara"], true)) {
        http_response_code(400);
        exit("Choose a listed city.");
    }
    setcookie("city", $city, [
        "expires" => time() + 3600, "path" => "/",
        "httponly" => true, "samesite" => "Lax"
    ]);
    $queued = $city;
}
header("Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8");
echo "Incoming city: $incoming\n";
if ($queued !== null) {
    echo "Queued for NEXT request: $queued\n";
}

programs.out:
# 1. First response queues a cookie; incoming array is still empty
$ curl -i -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d 'city=Surat' 'http://localhost/city.php'
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Host: 127.0.0.1:39093
Date: Thu, 29 Oct 2026 05:44:44 GMT
Connection: close
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.4.27
Set-Cookie: city=Surat; expires=Thu, 29 Oct 2026 06:44:44 GMT; Max-Age=3600; path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8

Incoming city: (missing)
Queued for NEXT request: Surat

# 2. Browser returns the saved cookie
$ curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt 'http://localhost/city.php'
Incoming city: Surat

# 3. Updating does not rewrite this request's cookie array
$ curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d 'city=Vadodara' 'http://localhost/city.php'
Incoming city: Surat
Queued for NEXT request: Vadodara

# 4. The updated value arrives on the next request
$ curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt 'http://localhost/city.php'
Incoming city: Vadodara

expl.en: A response's Set-Cookie header asks the browser to save a value; only a later request returns it in $_COOKIE. Updating uses the same name and path. Four genuine requests show missing → Surat → incoming Surat while queuing Vadodara → Vadodara. The shared -b/-c cookies.txt file is curl's browser memory. On production HTTPS also set secure => true; these local HTTP demos omit it.

title.en: Delete a cookie using the matching path

code.en:
<?php
$old = $_COOKIE["demo"] ?? "(missing)";
$action = $_POST["action"] ?? "read";
$options = [
    "path" => "/", "httponly" => true,
    "samesite" => "Lax"
];
if ($action === "set") {
    setcookie("demo", "BusBook", [
        "expires" => time() + 3600, ...$options
    ]);
} elseif ($action === "clear") {
    setcookie("demo", "", [
        "expires" => time() - 3600, ...$options
    ]);
}
header("Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8");
echo "Action: $action\n";
echo "Incoming demo: $old\n";
if ($action === "clear") {
    echo "Deletion queued; the next request proves it.\n";
}

programs.out:
# 1. Store the cookie
$ curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d 'action=set' 'http://localhost/clear_cookie.php'
Action: set
Incoming demo: (missing)

# 2. Confirm it returned
$ curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt 'http://localhost/clear_cookie.php'
Action: read
Incoming demo: BusBook

# 3. Expire the same name/path cookie
$ curl -i -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d 'action=clear' 'http://localhost/clear_cookie.php'

Host: 127.0.0.1:43097
Date: Thu, 29 Oct 2026 05:44:44 GMT
Connection: close
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.4.27
Set-Cookie: demo=deleted; expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:01 GMT; Max-Age=0; path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8

Action: clear
Incoming demo: BusBook

$ curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt 'http://localhost/clear_cookie.php'

Incoming demo: (missing)

expl.en: Cookie identity includes name, domain and path. Expire that same cookie in the past; unset($_COOKIE['demo']) alone would only change a PHP array for one request. The clear response still prints the incoming old value, then the next GET prints missing. Its genuine header shows an expired cookie with Max-Age=0.

code.en:
<?php // ===== File: booking.php =====
session_start();
$_SESSION["visits"] = ($_SESSION["visits"] ?? 0) + 1;
$_SESSION["seats"] ??= 0;
if ($_SERVER["REQUEST_METHOD"] === "POST"
    && ($_POST["add"] ?? "") === "seat") {
    $_SESSION["seats"]++;
}
header("Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8");
echo "Booking-page visits: ", $_SESSION["visits"], "\n";
echo "Reserved seats: ", $_SESSION["seats"], "\n";
echo "Open cart.php to read the same session.\n";

<?php // ===== File: cart.php =====
session_start();
header("Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8");
echo "Cart reads visits: ", $_SESSION["visits"] ?? 0, "\n";
echo "Cart reads seats: ", $_SESSION["seats"] ?? 0, "\n";

programs.out:
# 1. First booking-page visit
$ curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt 'http://localhost/booking.php'

Reserved seats: 0
Open cart.php to read the same session.

# 2. Add a seat using the same session
$ curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d 'add=seat' 'http://localhost/booking.php'

Open cart.php to read the same session.

# 3. Another PHP page reads the saved values
$ curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt 'http://localhost/cart.php'
Cart reads visits: 2
Cart reads seats: 1

# 4. A different browser has its own empty cart
$ curl 'http://localhost/cart.php'
Cart reads visits: 0
Cart reads seats: 0

expl.en: Save each labelled section as its own file. Every participating page calls session_start() before output. PHP sends a random session ID cookie, while visits and seats stay server-side. The cart page resumes the same record using that ID; a fresh browser has no seat reservation. This is a state demonstration, not an actual payment or inventory system.

title.en: unset, session_unset and full session destruction

code.en:
<?php
session_start();
$action = $_POST["action"] ?? "read";
if ($action === "set") {
    $_SESSION["user"] = "Ravi";
    $_SESSION["theme"] = "dark";
} elseif ($action === "remove-theme") {
    unset($_SESSION["theme"]);
} elseif ($action === "clear-values") {
    session_unset();
} elseif ($action === "destroy") {
    $_SESSION = [];
    if (ini_get("session.use_cookies")) {
        $p = session_get_cookie_params();
        setcookie(session_name(), "", [
            "expires" => time() - 3600,
            "path" => $p["path"],
            "domain" => $p["domain"],
            "secure" => $p["secure"],
            "httponly" => $p["httponly"],
            "samesite" => $p["samesite"] ?? "Lax"
        ]);
    }
    session_destroy();
}
header("Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8");
echo "Action: $action\n";
echo "User: ", $_SESSION["user"] ?? "(none)", "\n";
echo "Theme: ", $_SESSION["theme"] ?? "(none)", "\n";
echo "Active session: ",
     session_status() === PHP_SESSION_ACTIVE ? "yes" : "no",
     "\n";

programs.out:

$ curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d 'action=set' 'http://localhost/session_tools.php'

Theme: dark

$ curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d 'action=remove-theme' 'http://localhost/session_tools.php'

# 4. Seed again before full logout
$ curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d 'action=set' 'http://localhost/session_tools.php'
Action: set
User: Ravi
Theme: dark
Active session: yes

# 5. Clear values, expire cookie and destroy server data
$ curl -i -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d 'action=destroy' 'http://localhost/session_tools.php'
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Host: 127.0.0.1:46197
Date: Thu, 29 Oct 2026 05:44:44 GMT
Connection: close
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.4.27
Expires: Thu, 19 Nov 1981 08:52:00 GMT
Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate
Pragma: no-cache
Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=deleted; expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:01 GMT; Max-Age=0; path=/
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8

Action: destroy
User: (none)
Theme: (none)
Active session: no

$ curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt 'http://localhost/session_tools.php'

expl.en: Three different operations: unset removes one key; session_unset() clears all variables but leaves the session active; full logout clears $_SESSION, expires the session cookie using its original parameters, and calls session_destroy() to remove server-side data. The final request starts a new empty session, not the old user's record.

expl.en:
Save four separate files: login.php, config.php, dashboard.php and logout.php in one folder. Demo credentials: ravi / demo@123. The sample hash is generated from that lab password; real applications store a previously generated hash in the database, never hard-code real credentials.

The config starts a strict, cookie-only session before HTML. Login checks a CSRF token and password_verify(), regenerates the session ID on success, stores the user's name, then redirects. Dashboard checks authentication on every request; logout only accepts a valid-token POST, clears server state and expires the cookie. Secure is enabled automatically on direct HTTPS; configure it explicitly for your deployment if HTTPS terminates at a proxy.

The transcript proves guest denied → wrong password denied → correct password accepted → dashboard visible → logout → dashboard denied again. CSRF tokens are extracted from the actual forms for subsequent curl submissions. Random IDs and tokens change each run.

title.en: try, throw, catch and finally: fare division (Practical 18)

code.en:
<?php
function farePerPassenger(float $total, int $count): float {
    if ($count <= 0) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException(
            "Passenger count must be positive."
        );
    }
    return $total / $count;
}
foreach ([3, 0] as $count) {
    echo "Passengers: $count\n";
    try {
        echo "  checking...\n";
        $fare = farePerPassenger(900, $count);
        echo "  Fare each: Rs $fare\n";
        echo "  this line runs only on success\n";
    } catch (InvalidArgumentException $e) {
        echo "  Rejected: ", $e->getMessage(), "\n";
    } finally {
        echo "  finally: request finished\n";
    }
    echo "  continues after try/catch\n\n";
}

programs.out:
$ php index.php
Passengers: 3
  checking...
  Fare each: Rs 300
  this line runs only on success
  finally: request finished
  continues after try/catch

Passengers: 0
  checking...
  Rejected: Passenger count must be positive.
  finally: request finished
  continues after try/catch

expl.en: Normal case: all try statements run, catch is skipped, finally runs. Zero-passenger case: the function throws before dividing; the remaining try statements are skipped, the matching catch handles the exception, and finally still runs. The outer loop then continues. This deliberately throws an InvalidArgumentException; an unguarded PHP division by zero instead raises a DivisionByZeroError.

code.en:
<?php
class SeatsUnavailable extends RuntimeException {}

function reserveSeats(int $wanted, int $available): string {
    if ($wanted <= 0) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException(
            "Request at least one seat."
        );
    }
    if ($wanted > $available) {
        throw new SeatsUnavailable(
            "Only $available seats remain; wanted $wanted."
        );
    }
    return "Reserved $wanted seats.";
}
foreach ([2, 0, 5] as $wanted) {
    echo "Want $wanted:\n";
    try {
        $result = reserveSeats($wanted, 3);
        echo "  $result\n";
    } catch (SeatsUnavailable $e) {
        echo "  Availability: ", $e->getMessage(), "\n";
    } catch (InvalidArgumentException $e) {
        echo "  Input: ", $e->getMessage(), "\n";
    } catch (Exception $e) {
        echo "  Unexpected: ", $e->getMessage(), "\n";
    } finally {
        echo "  Booking attempt finished.\n\n";
    }
}

programs.out:
$ php index.php
Want 2:
  Reserved 2 seats.
  Booking attempt finished.

Want 0:
  Input: Request at least one seat.
  Booking attempt finished.

Want 5:
  Availability: Only 3 seats remain; wanted 5.
  Booking attempt finished.

expl.en: A domain-specific class (SeatsUnavailable extends RuntimeException) lets the caller distinguish sold-out routes from bad input. Catch specific types before a parent such as Exception: only the first matching catch executes. A broad parent placed first would swallow the custom case. In production, log internal failures and show a safe generic message rather than exposing paths or stack traces.

title.en: finally closes a file on success and failure

code.en:
<?php
function readManifest(string $path, bool $reject): void {
    $h = null;
    try {
        if (!is_readable($path)) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Manifest unavailable.");
        }
        $h = fopen($path, "r");
        if ($h === false) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Cannot open manifest.");
        }
        echo "  File opened.\n";
        if ($reject) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Manifest failed validation.");
        }
        echo "  Passenger: ", trim(fgets($h)), "\n";
    } catch (RuntimeException $e) {
        echo "  Handled: ", $e->getMessage(), "\n";
    } finally {
        if (is_resource($h)) {
            fclose($h);
            echo "  finally: file closed\n";
        } else {
            echo "  finally: no open handle\n";
        }
    }
}
$file = __DIR__ . "/manifest.txt";
file_put_contents($file, "Ravi Patel\n");
echo "1. Success\n";
readManifest($file, false);
echo "2. Failure AFTER open\n";
readManifest($file, true);
echo "3. Failure BEFORE open\n";
readManifest(__DIR__ . "/missing.txt", false);
unlink($file);

programs.out:
$ php index.php
1. Success
  File opened.
  Passenger: Ravi Patel
  finally: file closed
2. Failure AFTER open
  File opened.
  Handled: Manifest failed validation.
  finally: file closed
3. Failure BEFORE open
  Handled: Manifest unavailable.
  finally: no open handle

expl.en: One cleanup path for three genuine cases: normal read, exception after opening, and missing file before opening. Initialise the handle, test is_resource(), and close in finally. Many file functions warn/return false rather than throwing; test the return and throw deliberately when your application needs exception flow. finally normally runs even with return or a propagated exception, but not after exit() or process termination.

title.en: Exception vs Error: catching Throwable in modern PHP

code.en:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

function doubleSeats(int $n): int {
    return $n * 2;
}
$jobs = [
    "App exception" => function () {
        throw new RuntimeException("Payment service unavailable.");
    },
    "Division error" => function () {
        return 10 / 0;
    },
    "Type error" => function () {
        return doubleSeats("two");
    },
];
foreach ($jobs as $label => $job) {
    echo "$label:\n";
    try {
        $job();
    } catch (Exception $e) {
        echo "  Exception branch: ", get_class($e), "\n";
    } catch (Error $e) {
        echo "  Error branch: ", get_class($e), "\n";
    } finally {
        echo "  cleaned up\n";
    }
}
echo "Broad handler:\n";
try {
    doubleSeats("two");
} catch (Throwable $t) {
    echo "  Throwable also catches ", get_class($t), "\n";
}

programs.out:
$ php index.php
App exception:
  Exception branch: RuntimeException
  cleaned up
Division error:
  Error branch: DivisionByZeroError
  cleaned up
Type error:
  Error branch: TypeError
  cleaned up
Broad handler:
  Throwable also catches TypeError

expl.en: PHP 7+ has two throwable families: application Exception and engine Error (including TypeError and DivisionByZeroError). Both implement Throwable. catch (Exception $e) does not catch an Error; catch (Throwable $t) can handle either. Ordinary warnings/notices are not automatically exceptions. Handle expected failures close to the cause; a broad Throwable handler is a last safety boundary, not a reason to ignore programming bugs.

title.en: Cookie Lifecycle: Same Name and Path
Session ID Travels; Session Data Stays
Login to Logout: The Session Gate

terms.en: Set before output; read the new value on the next request.

items.f:
Same name + domain + path:
setcookie(name, newValue, opts)
Delete with a past expiry:
"expires" => time() - 3600
unset($_COOKIE[...]) is local only

terms.en: A different path can create a second cookie instead of replacing the first.

items.f:
"secure"   => true   // HTTPS
"httponly" => true   // no JS read
"samesite" => "Lax"
"path"     => "/"
Validate all incoming values.

terms.en: Production HTTPS: protect transport and minimise scope. Local HTTP demos do not require Secure.
Browser carries the ID; server stores the session values.
Removing values is not the same as destroying the session or expiring its cookie.
Three jobs: clear current values, remove browser cookie, destroy server data. See the complete program.
Start before output. Use password_verify, CSRF tokens and HTTPS in the complete app.
A throw skips the rest of try. Escape messages if rendering untrusted text as HTML.
Only the first matching catch executes; broad parents belong last.

items.f:
Throwable
  Exception -> RuntimeException
  Error     -> TypeError
            -> DivisionByZeroError
catch (Throwable $t) { ... }

terms.en: Exception does not catch Error. Ordinary warnings/notices are not automatically exceptions.

q.en: Why do web applications need cookies or sessions?

a.en: HTTP is stateless: separate requests do not automatically remember earlier choices or authentication. Cookies/sessions provide continuity.

q.en: What is a cookie?

a.en: A small name/value record stored by the browser for a site and sent with requests that match its scope and policy.

q.en: Which two HTTP headers implement the cookie round trip?

a.en: The server sends Set-Cookie in a response; the browser later sends Cookie in a request.

q.en: Why is a newly set cookie missing from $_COOKIE in the same request?

a.en: setcookie queues an outgoing response header; $_COOKIE contains the values from the incoming request. Read the new cookie on the next request.

q.en: How do you read a cookie without an undefined-key warning?

a.en: Use $_COOKIE['name'] ?? 'default', or check isset($_COOKIE['name']) before reading it.

q.en: How do you update a cookie?

a.en: Call setcookie again with a new value and the same name, domain and path. A different path can create another cookie.

q.en: How do you delete a cookie?

a.en: Expire it in the past using the same name, domain and path. The browser stops returning it on later requests.

q.en: Why is unset($_COOKIE['x']) not browser-side deletion?

a.en: It only removes the element from the PHP array for this request; it sends no Set-Cookie deletion header.

q.en: Why must setcookie run before HTML or echo?

a.en: It changes HTTP headers, which must be sent before the response body. Leading whitespace or a BOM can also cause headers-already-sent problems.

q.en: Persistent cookie vs browser-session cookie?

a.en: A persistent cookie has a future expiry timestamp; expiry 0/omitted creates a browser-session cookie. Browser policy and session restore affect actual retention.

q.en: Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite - what does each do?

a.en: Secure restricts sending to HTTPS; HttpOnly blocks JavaScript reading the cookie; SameSite controls cross-site sending. They protect different aspects and do not replace all other security checks.

q.en: Can an application trust a cookie saying role=admin?

a.en: No. Cookie values are client-controlled. Authenticate and authorise using validated server-side data; never store raw passwords in cookies.

q.en: What is a PHP session?

a.en: Server-side per-visitor storage normally selected by an opaque ID carried in a browser cookie.

q.en: What does PHPSESSID contain?

a.en: Normally a random session identifier, not the user's name, password or cart data. The ID maps to a server-side session record.

q.en: What does session_start do on a second page?

a.en: It resumes the existing session if a valid incoming ID is available, otherwise creates one. Call it before output on every participating page.

q.en: Can $_SESSION hold an array?

a.en: Yes. Session values can include arrays, strings, numbers and other serialisable application data; they are not limited to cookie-style string values.

q.en: Do two browsers normally share one session?

a.en: No. Separate cookie jars normally carry different session IDs and select separate server-side records.

q.en: unset($_SESSION['x']) vs session_unset()?

a.en: unset removes one named key. session_unset clears all variables in the active session, but does not destroy its identity or delete its cookie.

q.en: Does session_destroy automatically empty $_SESSION and delete its cookie?

a.en: No. It destroys server-side session data. Clear the current array and explicitly expire the matching cookie as separate steps.

q.en: List the steps of full logout.

a.en: Start/resume the session; clear $_SESSION; expire the session cookie using its original parameters; call session_destroy; redirect and exit.

q.en: What does session_regenerate_id(true) do?

a.en: Creates a new session ID while preserving current values, and deletes the old session data. Use after successful authentication to reduce fixation risk.

q.en: Session fixation vs session hijacking?

a.en: Fixation makes a victim use an attacker-known ID before authentication. Hijacking steals an already valid ID. ID regeneration, strict mode, HTTPS and cookie protections address different parts of these risks.

q.en: Why enable session.use_strict_mode and cookie-only IDs?

a.en: Strict mode rejects uninitialised supplied IDs; cookie-only IDs avoid leaking session identifiers through URLs. They are useful defaults, not a complete security solution.

q.en: How is a PHP page protected after login?

a.en: Start/resume the session and test a server-set authentication key before any private output. If missing, redirect to login and exit; hiding a link is not access control.

q.en: Is closing the browser a reliable logout mechanism?

a.en: No. Session restore may preserve cookies, and server records may remain. Enforce idle/absolute expiry explicitly and implement full logout.

q.en: What if a browser rejects the session cookie?

a.en: In a cookie-only configuration it cannot normally retain the same session across independent requests. Do not work around this by exposing IDs in URLs.

q.en: What is a CSRF token and where is it checked?

a.en: A random value stored in the session and included in a form; the server compares it on POST, for example with hash_equals. It helps reject forged state-changing requests.

q.en: Name the four main exception-handling keywords.

a.en: try surrounds risky work, throw signals failure with an object, catch handles a matching type, and finally performs cleanup.

q.en: What happens to statements after a throw inside try?

a.en: They are skipped. PHP searches for a compatible catch; cleanup in finally normally runs before control continues or the exception propagates.

q.en: Why must specific catches precede parent classes?

a.en: Only the first matching catch runs. A broad Exception catch placed first would absorb its subclasses and prevent more specific handling.

q.en: How do you obtain an exception's message and location?

a.en: getMessage() returns its description; getCode(), getFile() and getLine() provide diagnostics. Keep internal locations out of public error pages.

q.en: Why use finally instead of cleanup at the end of try?

a.en: An exception can skip the remaining try statements. finally provides a shared cleanup path for success and failure, including a normal return.

q.en: Does finally run under absolutely every circumstance?

a.en: No. It normally runs for return and propagated exceptions, but exit/die or process termination can prevent it. Avoid return inside finally because it can override a pending result or exception.

q.en: How do you define a custom exception?

a.en: Extend Exception or a suitable subclass, for example class SeatsUnavailable extends RuntimeException {}. Throw an instance and catch that specific class.

q.en: What is rethrowing?

a.en: A catch can use throw $e to pass the failure to an outer handler after local logging or other handling.

q.en: Will catch(Exception) automatically handle fopen warnings?

a.en: No. Many functions emit warnings and return false rather than throw. Check the return value and deliberately throw if your application requires exception flow.

q.en: Exception vs Error in PHP 7+?

a.en: They are distinct families. Application exceptions usually extend Exception; engine failures such as TypeError and DivisionByZeroError extend Error. Exception does not catch Error.

q.en: What does catch(Throwable $t) catch?

a.en: Both Exception and Error objects, since both implement Throwable. It does not automatically catch ordinary warnings or notices.

q.en: What happens if no matching catch exists?

a.en: The exception propagates to callers, with finally cleanup during normal unwinding. If still unhandled at the top level, the request terminates.

q.en: Should a production site display a complete stack trace?

a.en: No. Log useful diagnostics securely and show a safe user-facing message. Do not silently ignore failures or reveal internal paths, credentials or traces.

Write the code to destroy a cookie. Explain matching name/domain/path and why unset($_COOKIE['x']) is insufficient.
Compare cookies and PHP sessions in terms of storage, request transport, capacity, lifetime, trust and suitable uses.
